As someone who grew up playing EverQuest I am a huge fan of games that force long term (2 hours+) collaboration with similar people over prolonged periods of time (2-3 weeks at a time) and encourages socialization and collaboration.

For example, in EverQuest, a MMORPG, you had a limited number of zones you could fight in at particular levels. The game was designed in a way in which groups would set up "camps" where all members of the group would set up in a safe place and one person would pull enemies/monsters to the group. Typically groups would last a few hours and when one person would leave another would cycle in keeping the group functional. People would often spend a few weeks in the same zone leveling up.

Because of all of the above it was a perfect storm of seeing and working with the same people over a few weeks and having just enough time to converse between fighting together. This lead to some great social bonding and was the basis on which a lot of the original guilds started.

I have yet to see a game replicate this well. I think it is, in part, due to the way mobs are "teathered" now preventing the ability to set up camps. You have to all be constantly on the move so there is less time to interact. Further, a lot of games these days seem to focus on quests as the primary source of experience. Which means that people just grind quests but if you dont have the exact quests another person has you are going to, at best, team up for one quick quest, and then run your own directions. Horrible social design in my opinion.

Yep, Everquest was so good in ways it never gets credit for. I am 100% with you on the collaboration thing. If you want to get something done in that game, well, you better find some friends. And not just short-term friends either. The game got (forced) people to build social groups and friendships that endure to this day. "B-b-but," you say, " Warcraft was the same. I had friends there." Not like EQ, you didn't. The friendships in EQ were forged in fire, and tempered in the furnace of strife. The intense challenge, and penalties for failure, made who you grouped with absolutely crucial. A person with a bad reputation, in any way, be it skill with their class or abrasive personality, might as well stop playing.

Also, EQ is my favorite example of "meaningful downtime." The lulls in the gameplay-loop made such socializing possible. The time spent recovering from fights was not empty time. Bonds were formed then, laughs were had, and you learned even before level 20 who you would be playing with at level 50.

Some games that I think meet these criteria are XCOM, Shogun 2: Total War, Dwarf Fortress, Football Manager, and Age of Wonders 3.

Story and characters are more liabilities than assets -- done badly they make it difficult to enjoy a game, but done well they don't add much. They also can't stand up to repetition, assuming they're static. Playing through a game a second time and dealing with exactly the same story is a burden. Voice acting is expensive, so character voice clips tend to get repeated over and over. Games often commit to fully voiced dialogue, limiting how many different things characters can say. I sharply distrust games promoted as stories or emotional experiences, because I think the stories and emotional experiences in games should come from playing them, and not be predetermined and the same for everybody. Dwarf Fortress creates great stories, without having a canonical story, without even having a canonical world.

The more I am here the more I am liking the fact that there are point limits on certain global actions. I am coming around on the post limit and am definitely in favor of the 20 point limit for upvotes and 100 point for downvotes.

However, I was curious what people thought of the idea of turning the points into a currency of sorts? Where everyone gets a base number of upvotes, downvotes, links, and discussions they can use and then they earn more through positive actions that receive upvotes.

So right now it is 3 posts per hour per sub with a limit of 10 posts per sub per day, if I recall correctly.

What if someone who has a certain positive threshold of points for the past week they got 4 per hour and 12 per day and someone with a certain negative threshold they got 2 per hour and 6 per day. Or something to that effect.

This would very strongly encourage quality posting while not tipping the balance of power so strongly as to create power users. Obviously those numbers are just ones I pulled out of my ass based on the experimental quota numbers at the moment, the final balance of things would likely be very different.

Again, similar things could be applied to a large number of aspects of the site. I would be weary about limiting the number of comments people can make in general but maybe if someone has a certain threshold of downvotes over the past 7 days their timer between posting comments could increase, and likewise if the person has a certain threshold of upvotes the timer could be decreased.

This could all be based around the point system and I am sure it could be worked out in a way so that people were spending the points they have earned through positive action. Kind of like the partner program but for in site stuff rather than some monetary reward.

Rough idea, would definitely need to be fleshed out a bunch more, but what do you all think in general?

Edit: Part of why I am thinking of it this way is the distinction between upvotes being an indication of the value of content. If there were some cost associated with giving upvotes to people then they will be more thoughtful in what they vote up. The same thing applies to the limit on how many links you can post, presumably if you are limited to only a few posts per day then you are going to post only the best links you can for the day, rather than just the first stuff you come across.

Youtubers are often better knowledgeable on games then so-called "journalists" but are as susceptible to corruption as GJP was. Publications adopting ethics policies is great. Consumer advocacy groups could be a good idea but require a lot of money and clout to make possible.

Many gamers seem to have a lot of opinions on the games industry but stay confined with chans leaving the greater public at large uniformed. If we truly want a paradigm shift, I propose we start independently advocating on behalf of the consumer without relying on others. Not only will this empower consumers on an individual basis while providing insight from people who actually have a stake in the market, but it could also provide the financial clout necessary for forming consumer advocacy groups.

We can do this by starting our own blogs and video channels. Using google ads or crowd-funding can help support these advocates who can also link back to eachother so as many voices are heard as possible. Essentially, take a page from William Usher and go your own way.

Patreon is perhaps a good system for collecting revenue, despite how shitty their community guidelines are (http://gamergate.me/2015/02/patreon-community-guidelines/)). There are other problems with using Patreon, but so long as specific benchmarks are met it should be a viable service:

1) Charge Patrons by content, not by month. Paying per-content can always be revoked by the backer if they find the quality of a video or article is not up to snuff. In addition, this prevents creators from getting paid by merely existing.

2) Set milestone goals to encourage more donations. Collecting money without improving quality of production is a bad practice. This focuses on improvement and gives good reason for collecting money.

3) Disclose finances for supporting the website. Let everyone know exactly how much you are making, how much each of your backers are paying you, and where the money is going. This way you remain ethical.

4) Do not fund other Patreons. Currently there is a big confidence scheme going on throughout Patreon. You pay a friend, friend pays you back, and it ends up being a giant circle-jerk. By not backing eachother you boost your own credibility and avoid group-think.

The main benefits of Patreon are ease of convenience, disclosure, and branding. There is also a strong possibility of siphoning funds from trust fund babies by invading their platform.

Alternatively, you can use Gratipay, a services which 8chan uses, which provides a weekly siphon provided by willing backers.

Alternatively or in addition to, there is also good old fashioned Google AdSense to take advantage of.
